value.overview: The Striated Heron (Butorides striata) is a small, compact waterbird of the heron family. It is usually found alone along quiet freshwater and coastal margins, where it waits motionless before striking at prey. The species has a broad distribution across tropical regions of the Americas, Africa, and Asia. In Costa Rica, it is recognized as part of the national heron fauna and occurs mainly around suitable wetlands, rivers, streams, ponds, mangroves, and sheltered coastal waters.
value.classification: The Striated Heron belongs to the order Pelecaniformes and the family Ardeidae. Its scientific name is Butorides striata.
value.identification: This small heron has a short neck, rounded wings, a relatively short tail, and a long, pointed bill. Adults are generally dark gray or slate-colored above, with a darker crown, streaked neck and breast, and greenish or yellowish legs. Plumage varies geographically, and some individuals may appear browner or more richly colored. Juveniles are browner and more heavily streaked or spotted. It can resemble the closely related Green Heron, but range and plumage details help separate them.
value.rangeHabitat: The Striated Heron has a wide tropical and subtropical range extending through much of South America, Central America, parts of the Caribbean, Africa, and southern and eastern Asia. In Costa Rica, it is recorded as a resident heron rather than a regular long-distance migrant. It uses lowland and foothill wetlands, slow-moving rivers, forest streams, ponds, canals, mangroves, estuaries, and quiet coastal edges. Dense vegetation, overhanging branches, muddy margins, and shallow water provide important feeding and resting habitat.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica, with no regular seasonal migration pattern documented for the national population. Local movements may occur as water levels and food availability change.
value.breeding: The species usually breeds near water, often in trees, shrubs, mangroves, or other dense vegetation. It builds a loose platform nest from sticks, commonly positioned above or close to the water. The female typically lays a small clutch of pale bluish or greenish eggs, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Breeding timing varies across its broad range and is often linked to local rainfall and wet-season conditions. Costa Rica supports resident populations and likely local breeding where suitable habitat is available.
value.dietFeeding: Striated Herons feed mainly on small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects, frogs, tadpoles, and other small aquatic animals. They usually hunt from a low perch, exposed root, rock, or water-edge branch, remaining still before making a quick downward thrust with the bill. They may also walk slowly along muddy margins or shallow water. Like some related herons, individuals can occasionally use floating objects or other material to attract prey within striking range.
value.behavior: This is usually a solitary and secretive heron. It spends long periods standing quietly or crouched on a perch, then moves with sudden, deliberate actions when hunting. It is active during the day but may also feed at dawn, dusk, or under shaded conditions. When disturbed, it may fly low over the water and give a sharp call. Dense waterside vegetation is important for concealment, roosting, and escape from predators.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
